name: Amazon
description: Amazon's bar leans on Leadership Principles and scenario thinking more than raw algorithm difficulty. Coding rounds skew toward OOD and under-specified prompts that reward clarification skill, and a GenAI-usage behavioral question appears in nearly every modern loop. Bar Raiser independence and writing-heavy work samples shape the senior-level signal.

name: Apple
description: Apple interviews are unusually team-owned: the same company can run classic LeetCode screens, MLE case studies, hardware verification drills, project deep-dives, and system design loops with little advance disclosure. The strongest pattern is role fit: interviewers probe whether your prior work maps directly to the team's product surface, data domain, and engineering stack, while still expecting clean code, concise trade-off reasoning, and polished behavioral stories.

name: Google
description: Google's loop runs on hiring-committee arbitration, with a separate team-match phase deciding whether HC approval turns into an offer. Coding bars are remarkably consistent across teams; leveling rigor and behavioral depth drive most of the L3–L6 differentiation.

name: Uber
description: Uber's loop leans heavily on Uber Eats and rider/driver marketplace problems — Cart pricing, geo heatmaps, surge, and restaurant recommendation surface in nearly every onsite at L5+. Coding rounds are mostly tagged LeetCode patterns, but Hack2Hire OAs ship a small rotating set of original problems that rarely appear elsewhere. Coding bar is the gate; system design quality drives leveling between L5a / L5b / Senior / Staff.

name: Bytedance
description: ByteDance / TikTok runs a strict one-round-at-a-time funnel with sharp org-by-org variance in bar, language, and round mix. Coding rounds skew toward classic LeetCode-medium with one self-built test case; MLE and SRE loops front-load 30+ minutes of oral 八股 before any code is written. Interviewer professionalism varies — strong candidates drive the round structurally rather than waiting to be assessed.

name: Snowflake
description: Snowflake's loop is small and bank-driven: a recruiter screen, two back-to-back coding phone screens, then a virtual onsite that mixes coding, system design, and behavioral. The same handful of coding families (multi-source BFS on a grid, course-schedule variants, tree-node-deletion height problems, transactional KV stores) cycle through most candidates, so recognition speed matters more than novel problem solving.

name: Microsoft
description: Microsoft runs two parallel hiring tracks: the standardized Hiring Event (HE) loop covering Azure, Cloud, Copilot, and Office orgs, and Mustafa Suleyman's MAI org with its own recruiter pool and a distinctly OpenAI-flavored coding rotation. The HE bar is consistent — four 60-minute rounds back-to-back on a fixed weekday — with medium-difficulty algorithms and one system-design slot; MAI loops add project deep-dive depth and pull problems from an in-memory-DB / beam-search / streaming-decoder pool that does not overlap with classic LeetCode prep.

name: Karat
description: Karat conducts outsourced technical screens on behalf of hiring companies, so the round follows Karat's format rather than the hiring team's. Rounds are tightly time-boxed and multi-part, and reading speed on a long prompt or unfamiliar starter code matters about as much as coding speed.

name: Openai
description: OpenAI pairs an unusually high raw-coding bar with explicit no-AI-tools rules during most interviews — a deliberate contrast with the product. Phone screens often run a single multi-part simulation for the full hour, and senior loops add deep ML and research-grounded system-design rounds that probe mechanism, not vocabulary.

name: Meta
description: Meta sits mid-transition between two interview loops in 2026. The legacy track still drives most candidates through CodeSignal-style OAs and tightly time-boxed coding rounds, while a new AI-Native loop layers in AI-assisted coding, AI-Enabled system design, and an AI-oriented behavioral round on top. Which track you land in depends on org and recruiter, not candidate preference.

name: Oracle
description: Oracle's loops split along two clear axes: OCI (Cloud Infrastructure) runs a fairly standard LC + system-design loop with heavy Indian interviewer rotation, while OHAI (Oracle Health, the post-Cerner business unit) leans into OOD/class-design problems built around healthcare scenarios. Coding bars are mostly easy-to-medium, but interviewer variance and post-loop down-leveling / ghosting are unusually common — the loop result often determines the eventual level, not just the yes/no.

name: Capital One
description: Capital One's engineering loop is unusually predictable: a long CodeSignal OA gates everyone, then a single Power Day stitches four 45-60 minute rounds — coding, system design, case study, and behavioral — back to back. The technical bar is moderate but the case study and BQ rounds carry real weight, especially for MLE / Applied Research / Data Science where the business-context framing of a model decision is the differentiating signal.

name: Stripe
description: Stripe favors long realistic prompts in a full IDE — integration, debugging, refactor — over LeetCode-style algorithms. System design is grounded in payments and regulatory reality, and behavioral signals weigh ownership and written communication as heavily as raw technical depth.

name: C3.ai
description: C3 AI runs a compact, hiring-manager-led loop: a short behavioral conversation with the manager comes first, followed by a two-round onsite of coding and system design where design interviewers push hard on deep dives. New-grad Forward Deployed Engineer candidates start with a HackerRank assessment that blends CS fundamentals, applied-AI judgment, and practical coding.

name: Square
description: Block (Square, Cash App) screens with practical, multi-part CoderPad problems modeled on real product logic, where tests and clean refactoring between parts matter as much as the algorithm. Senior loops add a conversational round on AI-native engineering workflow, and money-movement teams probe correctness, legacy tech debt, and regulated-system judgment.

name: Waymo
description: Waymo loops mix nominally LeetCode-style coding with deliberately ambiguous, autonomy-flavored prompts and a signature 'data fluency' round that's hard to drill for. Coding bars are mid-hard but interviewers frequently swap in original problems framed around self-driving scenarios; ML and senior loops add a behavior-prediction-style ML system design round on top.

name: LinkedIn
description: LinkedIn's loop pivoted heavily in 2025 — Staff candidates now sit a packed two-round phone screen (coding + project retro) before a five-round onsite that includes an AI-Coding session in CoderPad's assistant pane. Behavioural depth is the dominant downlevel axis; the same coding bar that passes at Senior frequently caps a Staff loop with a downlevel offer.

name: Airbnb
description: Airbnb's loop is famously consistent and famously slow. The coding pool is small and reused — a candidate who has drilled the canonical questions (split-stay, terrain water-drop, KV store, code review) walks in advantaged. Differentiation happens in the code-review round, the experience deep-dive, and the standalone core-values round, which is calibrated separately from the rest of the loop and serves as a real gate. Expect strong technical performance to land in a multi-week team-match queue rather than a fast offer.

name: Roblox
description: Roblox interviews lean heavily on a small, stable repertoire of coding and system design prompts drawn from the company's own product surface — rate limiting, like-button counters, matchmaking queues, delayed payments. The bar is high but predictable: interviewers want bug-free implementations with crisp boundary handling and design discussions that ground every trade-off in real platform scale (millions of concurrent players, hot creator experiences, cross-region latency). HM and director rounds heavily probe past experience with comparable traffic and scope.

name: Pinterest
description: Pinterest's loop leans hard on a recurring custom prompt library — escape-room state-tracking, trie-backed access control, ads/log aggregation, splitwise-style settlement — over canonical LeetCode. ML system design is split into two distinct rounds ("ML Practitioner" and "ML System Design") that effectively cover the same recommender / retrieval / ranking surface from two angles, with embedding-heavy product framing throughout. Fully-remote, front-loaded compensation, and long team-match windows define the experience as much as the technical bar.

name: Disney
description: Disney hires through individual organizations such as Streaming and Experiences, and each hiring manager shapes the loop, so formats vary widely even for the same title. Coding is mostly practical and moderate in difficulty; project depth, collaboration, and trade-off-heavy design discussions carry most of the weight.

name: Netflix
description: Netflix's current engineering loop is high-signal and repeat-heavy: Ads candidates see the same topo / frequency-cap / ads data-modeling trio, Member-Commerce-Games candidates see homepage dedupe and duplicate-detection variants, and Infra / Data Platform candidates see cache, latency, and concurrency rounds. The technical prompts are usually solvable, but the grading is communication-heavy: candidates are expected to clarify vague requirements, write tests, explain trade-offs, and connect their past work tightly to the target org.

name: Citadel
description: Citadel and Citadel Securities run two distinct loops sharing one brand. Citsec (the market maker) hires for HFT software, quant research and quant dev; its phone screens lean on small, sharp coding prompts (merge-K, ring buffers, stock-DP ladders) and the loop is famously single-fail — any weak round and the next interview is cancelled within a day. Citadel (the hedge fund) and its sub-orgs (GQS, EQR, NXT) lean harder on probability brainteasers, deep resume drilling and a multi-week team-match stage where coding bar drops but cultural and PM-style fit dominates the offer decision.

name: Goldman Sachs
description: Goldman Sachs interview loops lean heavily on traditional LeetCode-style coding — the firm publishes its own tagged problem list on LeetCode, and the OA / phone screens recycle from a stable bank that maps closely to it. Behavioral signal is concentrated in a Hirevue video screen with tight 30-second prep windows, and quant-flavored desks (GSAM, Quant Engineering) layer probability and statistics drills on top of the standard coding bar.

name: Salesforce
description: Salesforce's loop is bank-driven: a small set of coding prompts (LFU Cache, Flatten JSON, linked-list dedup, frontend curry + traffic light, OA HackerRank classics) and one signature system design (Coffee Ordering, with its SQL follow-ups) cover the bulk of recent rounds. Down-leveling at offer time is common — the HM screen and behavioural depth materially shape the final level, often more than coding correctness alone.

name: Bloomberg
description: Bloomberg's loop is a coding-heavy gauntlet: three back-to-back technical rounds each pack two LeetCode-style problems with little hand-holding, plus an HR screen and an engineering manager round that anchors on a single deep project story. The coding bar emphasizes pristine communication — dry-running, edge cases, and complexity discussion are graded as heavily as the solution itself, and interviewers routinely push for second-best alternatives even after a working answer. New-grad and tech-screen verdicts often arrive within hours, while jump-shift onsites favor candidates who can explain past trade-offs without prompting.

name: NURO
description: Nuro builds autonomous driving technology and hires engineers who are as comfortable with threads and locks as with algorithms: its coding interviews deliberately split into a classic algorithm track and an OS-and-concurrency systems track. System design leans toward the realities of an autonomous fleet — heavy batch compute and enormous volumes of vehicle data — and the process extends past the onsite into meetings with senior leadership.

name: DoorDash
description: DoorDash's loop is dominated by a small, slow-moving library of original Code Craft prompts (Dasher Pay, Bootstrap API, Round Robin debugging) plus a handful of recurring system-design favorites (3-day Donation, Notification, Food Review). Coding bar is the gate; system design correctness and behavioral consistency drive leveling. The bar swings sharply with the interviewer — multiple candidates report bug-free coding rounds that still ended in rejection — so prepping the canonical question set cold matters more than chasing breadth.

name: Anthropic
description: Anthropic runs an unusually small, transparent technical question bank — the recruiter typically names which prompt family you'll see days before the round, so candidates can target preparation precisely instead of guessing. Bars are calibrated for problem-solving velocity and follow-up depth rather than novelty; offers are decided by hiring committee + reference check, and the culture round on AI-safety alignment is the single most common rejection point even for candidates who clear every technical stage.

name: Jump Trading
description: Jump Trading interviews engineers as low-latency systems builders: after a Codility screen, technical rounds favour hand-built infrastructure — interpreters, concurrent data structures, allocators — over puzzle-style algorithms. Quant research interviews are open-ended, centred on data reasoning and an unusually deep interrogation of past research.

name: Databricks
description: Databricks interviews are unusually bank-driven: candidates who know the recurring prompt families often recognize the round within the first few minutes. The loop mixes algorithmic coding with low-level systems and product-grounded design, then puts real weight on behavioral, hiring-committee, and reference signals after the technical rounds.

name: Jane Street
description: Jane Street hires through practical, conversational interviews rather than puzzle-bank recall. Engineering rounds are small, realistic programming tasks written without running code and judged on clarity and correctness, while trading and research loops rely on interactive games, live market making and probability reasoning under persistent questioning.

name: Anduril Industries
description: Anduril is a defense technology company, and much of its engineering work can only be done on-site, so roles are expected to be in the office. Interviews favor practical, quickly-solvable coding problems over puzzle-heavy ones, and the final round is often a hiring-manager conversation that rewards matching the scope the interviewer has in mind.

name: Dropbox
description: Dropbox's loop favors practical engineering over puzzle-solving: coding rounds start small and push toward scale and system concerns, and design interviewers probe implementation-level trade-offs. Ownership is tested hard, with a dedicated deep dive into a project you drove.

name: Pure Storage
description: Pure Storage (now also hiring under the Everpure name) reuses a small, well-known set of coding questions, so loops are decided by depth rather than novelty: interviewers press hard on concurrency, lock discipline and read/write optimization. Experienced loops close with a hiring-manager conversation and an architect-led design round built around real storage problems.

name: Snapchat
description: Snap interviews are highly interviewer-dependent: candidates report classic graph and cache problems, open-ended backend coding, product-heavy system design, and MLE loops that dig into recommendation systems, ranking, fundamentals, and project judgment. The safest preparation strategy is to be fluent in BFS/DFS, cache/data-structure implementation, feed and ads design, and concise behavioral stories around innovation, ambiguity, and execution.

name: Point72 Asset Management
description: Point72 hires across discretionary, systematic (Cubist) and data-heavy teams, and each role family runs its own loop. Engineering roles reward practical HackerRank fluency and broad, gap-free fundamentals; research roles test probability, statistics and portfolio-construction intuition alongside a close look at your own strategy work.

name: Whatnot
description: Whatnot is a live-stream shopping marketplace, and its engineering loop reflects that: engineers are expected to think like users of the app, with product sense assessed alongside coding and system design. Coding screens favor short, practical problems where finishing and testing the follow-ups matters more than algorithmic depth.

name: Optiver
description: Optiver is a market-making trading firm whose interview process is built to find fast, calibrated decision-makers under pressure. The funnel is dominated by a heavy online assessment — a probability/sequence/reaction battery for quant roles and OOP simulation coding for engineers — and the quant loop centers on a live EV betting game where speed and bet-sizing matter more than ending profit.

name: JPMorgan Chase
description: JPMorgan Chase's engineering loop is predictable but operationally uneven: a light HackerRank-style OA is followed by a Super Day with coding, code review, system design, and behavioral rounds rotating across candidates. The technical bar skews practical: simple algorithms, review of production-ish Java code, concurrency/style critiques, and system designs around traffic, search, inventory, payments, and URL routing.

name: Reddit
description: Reddit's loop runs on a small, slowly-rotating bank of company-specific coding prompts (Tennis Scoring, Report Chain, Chat Message Merge) paired with product-flavored system-design rounds (Game Leaderboard, Live Chat, Notification System). The bar is high on clean OOD and crisp clarification — multi-part prompts are routinely under-scoped on purpose, and rounds end without finishing all parts. Ads and ML Platform orgs add a hiring-manager domain round on top of the standard loop; recent cohorts also report aggressive down-leveling and long team-match limbo after a passing loop.

name: Adobe
description: Adobe has no single company-wide loop: each hiring team defines its own rounds, so a 'coding' interview can turn into system design and an ML screen can mean implementing an algorithm from scratch. Staff loops lean heavily on system design and operational maturity, while MLE loops range from traditional ML to LLM serving and GPU performance.

name: NVIDIA
description: NVIDIA interviews are highly team-specific and much less LeetCode-bank-driven than most large tech loops. System Software, Linux, Tegra, DGX AI infra, and Deep Learning roles lean toward engineering scenarios: C/C++ debugging, graph validation, GPU / inference fundamentals, small utility coding, and project deep dives; some design and product-facing AI roles add system-design or technical-marketing discussions.

name: Coinbase
description: Coinbase runs a long, gated pipeline — AI recruiter screen, a cognitive aptitude test, a culture/personality questionnaire, and a CodeSignal coding OA all precede the recruiter call, and team match still happens before the 4-round VO. Coding rounds bias toward multi-level CodeSignal-style problems (banking system, in-memory database, mining-block knapsack, crypto order management) over canonical LeetCode; bring your own scaffolding because interviewers often hand you a blank file with no class structure or tests. AI-assisted coding is now an explicit round on its own.

name: Tradedesk
description: The Trade Desk's interviews favor practical, simulation-style engineering over puzzle solving, from a levels-based CodeSignal assessment to live rounds drawn from a fixed internal question bank. System design is grounded in its ad-bidding business, where serving read-heavy data at extremely low latency across regions is the central concern.

name: Nextdoor
description: Nextdoor is a neighborhood-based social network, and its interviews stay close to that product: feeds, posts, comments, and the metrics behind them. The process opens with an unusually heavy two-round phone screen, and decisions are terse and opaque, so polish and speed count even on familiar problems.

name: Tesla
description: Tesla interviews are highly team-specific: Autopilot, Optimus, Dojo, data engineering, infotainment, and factory-software teams each run their own practical technical screens. The common pattern is a fast transition from resume/project discussion into runnable code, with interviewers pushing for optimality, clean implementation style, and concrete ownership of past technical decisions.

name: Confluent
description: Confluent runs a compact loop built on a small, recurring pool of practical, systems-flavored coding problems and product-style system design, where API and data-model clarity count for more than diagrams. Since joining IBM, hiring runs through IBM's channels and can include an extra values-alignment step.

name: AkunaCapital
description: Akuna Capital interviews lean heavily into the firm’s trading DNA: fast arithmetic, probability, market-making intuition, and implementation details that resemble exchange or trading-engine code. Quant roles can move through multiple asynchronous assessments before a superday, while developer tracks mix HackerRank-style coding, C++ debugging, data-structure design, and practical rate-limit or order-book exercises.

name: eBay
description: eBay interviews vary markedly by team, from practical code review and product implementation to algorithms and distributed-system design. Candidates may also be assessed on language-specific fluency and detailed discussion of previous projects.

name: Xai
description: xAI's loop is built around speed and founder-style intensity: a single 15-minute video screen often gates the entire pipeline, the take-home assumes you will use Cursor / Claude Code, and onsite rounds run in person in Palo Alto with offers decided minutes after the final round. Bars are calibrated less for algorithmic novelty than for raw shipping velocity, low-level systems instincts (concurrency, GPU/inference, distributed numerics), and willingness to work 60–100 hour weeks RTO5.

name: Walmart Global Tech
description: Walmart's engineering loop runs through Karat / HackerRank phone screens followed by a three-to-four round virtual or in-person onsite covering coding, system design, behavioral, and an extended Team Fit phase. Coding bars are moderate but heavily weighted toward Java / Spring Boot fluency, and the system-design slot leans toward retail and logistics prompts (membership, delivery, ticketing, sensor ingestion). The Team Fit phase that follows technical approval is unusually long and team-shopping in nature, and is responsible for a meaningful share of loop attrition.

name: Hudson River Trading
description: HRT interviews combine practical implementation with close examination of systems and language fundamentals. Software, infrastructure, and research paths can use substantially different assessments and onsite formats.

name: PayPal
description: PayPal's loop is built from 45-minute rounds that often pack two or three classic problems into one session, alongside resume-driven deep dives and a hiring-manager conversation. Interviewer style varies widely, so be ready to drive the conversation and move fast.

name: Zoox
description: Zoox runs a remarkably stable loop: a language-trivia plus object-oriented coding phone screen, then an onsite where fast-paced coding sits alongside a hand-calculated math and physics round. Execution speed under tight time limits matters more than novelty, while design and deep-dive rounds shift sharply by team — from robotaxi backend to ML, GPU, and simulation.

name: Expedia
description: Expedia Group runs short loops — usually three to four virtual rounds — that pair one or two LeetCode-style coding rounds with design prompts drawn directly from the interviewing team's travel-domain work, such as partner connectivity, payments, and property data. Most rounds open with an Expedia-values question, and behavioral judgment carries as much weight as coding at senior levels.

name: Sig
description: Susquehanna International Group is a Philadelphia-based quantitative trading firm that hires through two distinct tracks. Quant candidates face a timed math-and-logic assessment, probability screens, and a data-driven strategy task. Software engineers see a short, stable rotation of practical coding and object-design problems, where deep, interviewer-specific follow-ups and team fit decide outcomes.

name: Glean
description: Glean builds enterprise search and work AI, and its interviews lean toward practical, implementation-heavy coding rather than puzzle tricks. ML candidates also face an ML design round and a build round paired with an AI coding assistant, so working fluently with AI tools is part of the bar.

name: Atlassian
description: Atlassian interviews emphasize pragmatic product engineering: API design, backend data structures, careful clarification, and values-driven collaboration. Senior loops add management-signal and leveling weight, while MLE loops still include substantial backend coding alongside recommendation, RAG, and ML systems design.

name: IBM
description: IBM's recent technical screens are dominated by auto-triggered HackerRank online assessments for entry-level, intern, full-stack, backend, AI, and .NET roles. The question mix is mostly easy-to-medium data structures, sliding-window, interval, graph-connectivity, and small frontend/CSS tasks, while Red Hat / AI-infrastructure loops add live coding around inference kernels, Kubernetes controllers, and DevOps fundamentals.

name: Visa
description: Visa's software loop pairs a strictly proctored HackerRank assessment with a one-day virtual interview event in which every round opens with a resume project deep dive. At Staff level the assessment itself is the main filter, built on twisted DP and graph variants; at Senior, project depth (especially AI work) and system design decide the outcome, and team match after the onsite is a real technical step.

name: Abnormalsecurity
description: Abnormal Security builds AI-driven email and collaboration security against phishing, business email compromise and account takeover. Its interviews skip LeetCode entirely: rounds pair an open engineering discussion with a hands-on exercise drawn from day-to-day work, rewarding practical judgment over algorithm drilling.

name: Applied intuition
description: Applied Intuition interviews combine practical software implementation with close examination of career decisions. Role-specific technical work and a strong emphasis on company fit shape both software and specialist loops.

name: Squarepoint
description: Squarepoint interviews vary substantially between software engineering, quantitative research, and discretionary trading. Practical implementation and technical fundamentals sit alongside role-specific mathematical and financial reasoning.

name: SoFi
description: SoFi's engineering interviews mix Karat-style screens, practical frontend builds, backend coding, and manager-led project depth. The loop rewards candidates who can clarify ambiguous product requirements, keep implementation details tidy under HackerRank or Karat constraints, and explain trade-offs without drifting away from the requested scope.

name: Notion
description: Notion's interviews are built around its own product: tables, documents with edit history, page permissions, to-do lists, and calendars. Coding rounds reward building a clean API quickly and then reasoning about caching, mutability, and scale. Offers often turn on fit with the specific team's stack and focus.

name: Upstart
description: Upstart combines tightly timed coding assessments with practical project work and experience discussions. Research and machine-learning interviews place additional emphasis on statistical reasoning, simulation, and hands-on modelling.

name: Cisco
description: Cisco's recent technical loops are split between automated OA batches for SWE / intern roles and Meraki-style phone or manager loops. The OA bank leans practical and implementation-heavy: strings, arrays, linked lists, grids, and small dynamic-programming tasks with strict output formatting.

name: Flexport
description: Flexport is a freight forwarder and customs broker building software for global trade. Its interviews lean on that domain: coding and design prompts are often framed as logistics scenarios, and design rounds put heavy weight on data modeling and API design.

name: Figma
description: Figma builds its interviews around its own product surface and runs them as collaborative, test-case-driven pair-programming sessions where candidates pick their own language and prompts are deliberately long and under-specified. Coding signal rewards clean handling of messy object models over algorithmic trickiness; system-design rounds reward pragmatic, right-sized solutions over over-engineering. Since the IPO the bar has tightened, and final leveling is often settled in a separate executive conversation.

name: HubSpot
description: HubSpot interviews favor practical engineering over puzzle-solving: level-gated online assessments, coding rounds built around real HTTP and JSON handling in your own environment, and product-style system design. Behavioral screens are short and anchored in the company's culture values, and technical rounds are often shadowed.

name: rippling
description: Rippling's engineering loop is unusually concentrated: a small set of OOD coding prompts, two data-heavy system-design prompts, and a practical web API round account for most SWE interviews. The bar is driven by speed through multi-part prompts, clean extensible design, and whether the candidate can collaborate with AI tools without losing ownership of the solution.

name: Tower Research
description: Tower Research Capital hires team by team across its trading groups, so the interview loop depends on the group you apply to rather than one firm-wide process. Expect rapid probability and statistics questions for research roles, practical coding graded on robustness and efficiency, and detailed resume probing by senior portfolio managers.

name: Perplexity
description: Perplexity interviews lean toward long, product-flavored engineering simulations rather than generic LeetCode. Candidates should expect Python-first coding, incremental multi-part specs, careful edge-case preservation across parts, and system-design conversations tied closely to search, discovery, retrieval, inference, and operational reliability.

name: Pinduoduo
description: Temu (Pinduoduo's overseas arm) runs a fast, recruiter-driven loop conducted largely in Chinese, where every technical round front-loads 20-40 minutes of detailed project deep dive and leaves only 10-20 minutes for an easy-to-medium LeetCode problem. There is no system-design round; for senior candidates the decisive gate is a final director/VP/SVP conversation that scrutinizes project depth and cross-round consistency far more than algorithms.

name: Grammarly
description: Grammarly, now also operating under the Superhuman name, runs a fast LeetCode-style HackerRank phone screen followed by a virtual onsite built around practical class-design coding, product-flavored system design and an unusually thorough resume deep dive. Rounds are eliminating — a miss usually cancels the rest of the loop — and feedback is rarely shared.

name: Okta
description: Okta runs a lightweight, team-driven loop with a fast weekly cadence — recruiter call, a short online assessment, one or two interviewer-watched coding rounds, and hiring-manager conversations, with offer decisions made at the team level rather than a central committee. Coding leans practical over heavily algorithmic, and the assessment stack is unusually AI-forward: recent OAs explicitly allow AI tools and lean on hands-on builds against Okta/Auth0's real identity APIs.

name: Kikoff
description: Kikoff is a consumer credit-building fintech, and its screens reflect that domain: practical parsing and verification tasks over vendor payloads and service logs, plus large-scale scoring design built on credit-bureau data. Asking the right clarifying questions counts as much as the code.

name: Two Sigma
description: Two Sigma's loops split sharply by track: QR and data roles emphasize linear models, statistics, data-analysis case work, and domain reasoning, while SWE/QSE loops favor implementation-heavy trading, database, data-structure, and OOD prompts. The process is fast, high-variance, and often unforgiving on incomplete code or unclear statistical reasoning.

name: Voleon
description: Voleon is a quantitative investment firm that applies machine learning to systematic trading. Its coding questions tend to be framed around trading infrastructure: order flow, position reconciliation, price data and node-to-node data sync.

name: Ramp
description: Ramp front-loads a CodeSignal "industry coding framework" online assessment — a four-level progressive object-modeling problem — often before any resume review, then runs a small, heavily-repeated set of live coding rounds. Prompts are deliberately under-specified: printing and exploring the data format yourself is the real signal, and the bar rewards fast, debuggable, pragmatic code over elegance. The loop also explicitly probes how you collaborate with AI tools.

name: Lyft
description: Lyft's engineering loop is hands-on and execution-heavy: candidates repeatedly see practical API-wrapper, in-memory data-store, scheduling, and product-system prompts rather than abstract puzzle rounds. Senior loops add system design around payments, donation flows, web crawling, or marketplace-adjacent products, while frontend and intern tracks lean toward small project-style implementation.

name: Shopify
description: Shopify's loop is unusually lightweight and behavior-heavy: a cognitive assessment and a long "life story" values interview gate most candidates before any real coding. The signature technical round is a 75-minute AI-assisted pair-programming session where bringing your own AI coding tool (Cursor, Claude Code, Cline, Copilot) is encouraged — the real test is communication, reviewing AI-generated code, edge-case handling, and testing rigor rather than algorithmic difficulty. MLE loops add ML modeling and ML system-design rounds built around Shopify's own product-taxonomy, forecasting, and recommendation problems.

name: Robinhood
description: Robinhood's loop leans on a small, stable bank of recurring problems: a graph load-factor / referral-count coding question, a Job Scheduler system design, and a stock-quote / trading-system design. Onsites pair these with a project deep dive that is graded as hard as the technical rounds, and interviewers consistently reward complete, edge-case-correct code over elegant-but-unfinished design.

name: Asana
description: Asana's engineering loop is built around object-oriented design: modeling games and puzzles shows up in the phone screen and again onsite, alongside a long solo build of a small stateful program. With a stable, well-known question set, interviewers weigh how clearly you reason and communicate trade-offs as much as whether the code works.

name: Samsara
description: Samsara builds IoT and fleet-operations software: vehicle telematics, connected cameras, and tooling for fuel, safety, and compliance. Its interviews favor practical, product-flavored problems over algorithm puzzles, with loosely specified parsing-style coding tasks and design rounds rooted in its own telematics systems, where UX and integration with existing APIs count as much as backend architecture.

name: Instacart
description: Instacart's recent SWE loop is dominated by CodeSignal-style practical coding: in-memory databases, worker/task trackers, expression parsing, file I/O, and product/inventory consistency. Senior loops now commonly split the onsite into two phases: two coding rounds plus a Karat AI codebase round first, then system design and project deep-dive if the first phase clears. MLE loops keep the same practical coding bar but add a fundamentals-heavy ML concept screen.

name: Wayfair
description: Wayfair is a Boston-based online retailer of furniture and home goods. Its ML interviews lean heavily on business and product judgment in e-commerce scenarios rather than on modeling depth. Its software loops pair practical coding with both a large-scale system design round and an object-oriented app design round.

name: Intuit
description: Intuit's recent engineering loop is unusually AI-aware: even standard SWE screens often pair a short practical coding task with a separate conversation about using generative AI safely and effectively. New-grad assessment traffic is dominated by mixed-format OA work across Python, SQL, and Bash, while experienced screens skew toward product-flavored implementation and applied data tasks.

name: MathWorks
description: MathWorks EDG interviews center on a structured early-career pipeline: HireVue motivation and sponsorship checks, a HackerRank OA with math plus coding or MATLAB, then technical rounds that mix OA review, easy-medium algorithms, OOD, and EDG fit. Preparation should cover non-Python OA languages, MATLAB awareness, project storytelling, and clear understanding of the EDG rotation/support model.

name: Verkada Inc.
description: Verkada interviews frequently connect coding and architecture to cameras, device health, and access permissions. Live engineering exercises can sit alongside algorithm questions, with a strong emphasis on explaining practical design choices.

name: Ziprecruiter
description: ZipRecruiter is an online job marketplace that uses ML-based matching to connect job seekers with employers. It is a public company headquartered in Santa Monica.

name: Circle
description: Circle's loop is compact and relies on a small, stable question pool. A CodeSignal OA leads into a three-round virtual onsite: system design, hands-on pair programming against a real database, and a hiring-manager conversation. Crypto fluency matters more here than at most companies, starting with the recruiter call.

name: Affirm
description: Affirm's loop leans on realistic fintech coding problems—loan aggregation, transaction reconciliation, fraud detection, promotion redemption—run on HackerRank with long boilerplate that rewards careful reading over algorithmic flash. System design centers on experimentation platforms and payment data models; hiring-manager rounds favor 'how did you' probing over scripted STAR. Expect strong signal on requirement comprehension and clean data-structure manipulation, plus a recruiting process that can be slow or go quiet.

name: ARM
description: Arm's early-career hardware and compiler pipelines usually open with a recorded video interview that pairs behavioral prompts with verbal technical questions tied to the team's domain, so preparation is about explaining fundamentals clearly rather than grinding generic coding. Verification roles add live rounds that weigh verification methodology alongside basic Python.

name: Bobyard
description: Bobyard builds AI-powered takeoff and estimating software for landscaping and construction contractors.

name: Palantir
description: Palantir interviews combine practical implementation, work with unfamiliar code, and discussion of how candidates make decisions. Company motivation and fit for the specific role can matter from the first recruiter conversation.

name: Baseten
description: Baseten is an AI infrastructure company that provides a platform for deploying, serving and scaling machine-learning models in production, with a focus on low-latency inference.

name: MongoDB
description: MongoDB interviews favor practical, database-flavored coding over puzzle-style problems, and judge candidates on production-quality code rather than just a working answer. Concurrency is a recurring theme across coding, code-review and design rounds, and low-level teams probe operating-system and networking internals in depth.

name: Weride
description: WeRide interviews pair coding with substantial discussion of prior engineering work. Team-specific language and systems depth can influence the outcome through the manager and team-matching stages.

name: Docker
description: Docker develops the container platform and developer tooling (Docker Desktop, Docker Hub, BuildKit) used to build, share, and run containerized applications.

name: HarveyAI
description: Harvey builds domain-specific generative-AI tools for law firms and legal teams, layering retrieval and document-workflow products (Vault / Data Room) on top of frontier LLMs. Its interview loop is small and stable: a single coding screen drawn from a tight rotation, system-design rounds anchored on Harvey's own document products, and a values-driven behavioral bar — with recruiters who actively prep candidates before each round.

name: Cursor
description: Cursor screens for engineers who can ship working code in a realistic environment: coding rounds run against a real repository and are judged on complete, self-tested solutions within the hour rather than on puzzle cleverness. The loop is sequential and practical throughout, with product-adjacent design, a project deep dive and a hiring-manager conversation leading to an in-person work trial.

name: Oscar Health
description: Oscar Health runs a compact engineering loop — one coding screen and a two-round onsite — and grounds its custom questions in its own health-insurance business: provider networks, physician licensing, member outreach. Design rounds come as terse written briefs, and candidates are expected to set the scope and drive the discussion themselves.

name: Hugging Face
description: Hugging Face is the open-source AI platform behind the Hub and libraries such as Transformers, Diffusers and TRL, hosting models, datasets and Spaces for the ML community.

name: Vanta
description: Vanta runs a deliberately small, stable interview loop built around a handful of recycled problems — a topological-sort phone screen, a local-machine `uniq` build, and an internal DAU/MAU analytics design. Difficulty skews easy-to-moderate, but the prompts are verbose and reading-comprehension-heavy, and most rejections trace to requirement-clarification or following the interviewer's instructions rather than raw algorithmic strength.

name: Scale.ai
description: Scale AI's recent engineering loops are practical and implementation-heavy: candidates are expected to write working code under shared-screen conditions, reason about production readiness, and explain prior ML or product work clearly. MLE loops add NumPy-level model implementation, LLM training theory, and paper or project trade-off discussions, while FDE and enterprise roles lean toward customer-facing AI systems.

name: Qualcomm
description: Qualcomm hires through team-run loops that differ sharply by discipline: LeetCode-style coding for software, deep fundamentals grilling for compiler and RF hardware. For many international candidates, export-control licensing weighs as heavily as interview performance.

name: Temporal
description: Temporal Technologies builds Temporal, an open-source durable execution platform for writing reliable workflows, plus the managed Temporal Cloud service.

name: Yahoo
description: Yahoo's ML interviews are practical and conversational: short NumPy exercises grounded in recommendation and ranking, textbook ML fundamentals, and deep dives into production projects you have owned. Software-engineering and intern rounds mix practical coding (finance-flavored data processing, classic string and hash-map problems, UI event handling in pseudo-code), CS-fundamentals checks and large-scale system design. Teams have shifted toward a faster-paced culture after recent reorganizations, and headcount can change mid-process.

name: Datadog
description: Datadog interviews use observability and developer-tooling scenarios across coding and architecture. Project explanation and role-specific depth can affect both progression and leveling, alongside implementation performance.

name: Merge
description: Merge provides unified APIs that let B2B software companies add hundreds of third-party integrations (HRIS, ATS, CRM, accounting and more) through a single API.

name: Canva
description: Canva is an online visual design platform used to create graphics, presentations, documents and videos, with a growing set of AI-powered design features.

name: Cartesia
description: Cartesia builds real-time voice AI, including low-latency text-to-speech models (Sonic) served through streaming APIs.

name: Inworld AI
description: Inworld AI builds generative AI infrastructure for real-time interactive characters and voice, used in games and consumer applications.

name: Quizlet
description: Quizlet is an online learning platform where students study with flashcards, practice tests and AI-powered study tools.

name: Chime
description: Chime runs a compact, fast-moving loop: one coding phone screen, then a four-round virtual onsite with coding, a fixed banking-domain system design, and two behavioral conversations. Clean technical execution is necessary but not sufficient. How you communicate and collaborate while solving problems weighs heavily in the final decision.

name: Parafin
description: Parafin is a fintech company that offers embedded financing, such as merchant cash advances, to small businesses through partner platforms.

name: Miro
description: Miro is a collaborative online whiteboard platform for teams to brainstorm, diagram and plan together on an infinite canvas.
